notes.meaning: One of Jesus' followers pulled out a sword and sliced off the ear of the high priest's servant. John's Gospel later tells us this disciple was Peter and the servant was named Malchus. Peter acted out of hasty courage, trying to defend his Master with force before Jesus gave any command to fight.

Jesus ordered Peter to put his sword back into its sheath. He warned that people who reach for the sword will end up being destroyed by the sword. God's kingdom cannot be defended or spread by weapons of violence.

differ.view: Christ forbids private revenge and unlawful violence, but He does not forbid lawful civil rulers and governments from using the sword to punish evil.
Christ teaches that His church and His kingdom must never be defended by military force or weapons of war, and private believers should not violently resist public officers.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Early church teachers held that Jesus gave this command to calm Peter's fiery anger and to show that He was giving Himself up willingly.

notes.meaning: Jesus reminded Peter that He did not need human weapons to protect Him. If He asked, His Father would instantly send more than twelve legions of angels to His side. A Roman legion had about six thousand soldiers, so a vast heavenly army was ready at a word. Jesus gave Himself up by choice, not out of weakness.

If Jesus were rescued by an army of angels, the Old Testament promises could not come to pass. The Scriptures had already foretold that the Savior must suffer and die to pay for human sin. Jesus chose obedience to God's rescue plan over His own safety.

Jesus asked the armed crowd why they came out with swords and clubs as if they were hunting down a dangerous bandit. He had sat openly in the temple courts teaching every day, and they never laid a hand on Him there. They came under the cover of night because they were afraid of the public.

All of this took place to fulfill what the ancient prophets had written about the Messiah's suffering. When the disciples realized that Jesus would not fight and was allowing Himself to be arrested, their courage vanished. Every single one of them deserted Him and ran into the dark.

The armed group marched Jesus to the residence of Caiaphas, the high priest. The scribes and elders were already waiting there in a late-night gathering to hold a hearing. They rushed the trial in secret so the crowds in Jerusalem would not find out and start a riot.

Peter followed Jesus from a safe distance all the way to the high priest's courtyard. Once inside, he sat down by the fire among the guards to watch what would happen. His love made him want to stay near, but his fear kept him from standing openly with his Lord.

The chief priests and the whole Jewish high council, called the Sanhedrin, tried hard to find false evidence against Jesus. They had already decided to put Him to death before the trial even began. Instead of acting as fair judges, they were hunting for any excuse that sounded legal.

Many people stepped forward to tell lies about Jesus, but their stories did not agree with each other. Jewish law required at least two matching witnesses before anyone could be sentenced to death. At last, two men came forward whose accusations seemed to line up.

The two witnesses claimed that Jesus said He could tear down God's temple and rebuild it in three days. They were twisting words Jesus had spoken years earlier about His own body being killed and raised from the dead. By bending His words, they tried to make Him look like a dangerous threat to the holy temple.

Caiaphas the high priest stood up in anger and asked Jesus why He had nothing to say. He was annoyed that the witnesses were so weak and that Jesus refused to answer their clumsy lies. Caiaphas hoped to provoke Jesus into saying something that could be used against Him.

Jesus kept silent, fulfilling the ancient prophecy that the suffering servant would not open His mouth. Caiaphas then placed Him under a binding legal oath by the living God. He demanded that Jesus tell them plainly whether He was the Christ, the Son of God.

Jesus answered that the high priest had said it correctly, confirming that He truly is the Messiah. He added that they would one day see the Son of Man seated at God's right hand of power and returning on the clouds of heaven. The humble prisoner warned His judges that He would one day return as their Judge.

differ.view: The phrase 'from now on' marks the contrast between Christ's humble earthly state and His future visible return in glory at the end of time.
The phrase refers to Christ's divine power becoming visible very soon after His resurrection, seen through the day of Pentecost and the spread of His kingdom.

notes.meaning: The high priest tore his own robes to show shock and horror, claiming Jesus had spoken blasphemy, which means insulting God's holy name. He told the council they no longer needed any other witnesses because they had heard the claim with their own ears.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Ancient church writers saw the high priest tearing his priestly robe as a sign that the Old Testament priesthood was being torn away and ended forever.

notes.meaning: Caiaphas called for a final vote, and the leaders all agreed that Jesus deserved to die. Under the Law of Moses, blasphemy carried the death penalty. Because the Jewish council did not have the power under Roman rule to carry out executions, they condemned Him here before handing Him over to the governor.

The men guarding Jesus spat right into His face to show their complete disgust. Others punched Him with their fists or slapped Him across the face. Jesus patiently bore this cruel abuse, fulfilling prophecies that the Savior would be beaten and disgraced for our sake.

After covering Jesus' eyes, the abusers laughed at His claim to be the Messiah and dared Him to prophesy who had just struck Him. They thought that if He were truly from God, He would be able to name them without looking. Jesus remained silent through their mockery.

While Jesus stood on trial inside, Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard. A servant girl walked over and called him out, saying he was one of the men who had been with Jesus the Galilean. This sudden question put Peter's loyalty to the test before ordinary servants.

Peter denied the claim right in front of everyone, saying he had no idea what the girl was talking about. Fear of being captured made him pretend he was a total stranger to Jesus. This cowardly lie was the first step in Peter's downward slide.

Peter slipped away from the fire and headed toward the entrance gate to avoid being noticed. Another servant girl spotted him there and told the crowd that this man had been with Jesus of Nazareth. Even though Peter tried to hide in the shadows, he could not escape recognition.

Peter denied Jesus a second time, and this time he swore an oath to back up his lie. He insisted that he did not even know the man, using cold words to cut all ties with his Teacher. His sin grew worse as he added a sacred vow to a dishonest denial.

About an hour later, the people standing around came up and pressed Peter again. They told him that he must be one of Jesus' followers because his Galilean accent gave him away. People from northern Galilee had a distinct regional way of talking that sounded different from the people of Jerusalem.

In a panic, Peter began calling down curses on himself and swearing that he did not know Jesus at all. Just as those words left his mouth, a rooster crowed in the early morning air. Peter had reached the very bottom of his fear and failure.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars argue that Matthew presents Peter as a true apostate who completely rejected discipleship, rather than just a faithful follower whose courage failed.

notes.meaning: The rooster's crow pierced Peter's heart and brought back the warning Jesus had given him hours earlier: before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times. Overcome with deep sorrow and shame, Peter rushed out into the dark and cried bitterly. His broken heart showed true repentance, and God later restored him.
